subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Five kinds of formula and how to interconvert them
The functional groups and the classes they define
Why boiling points rise along a series
Structural isomers, and primary, secondary, tertiary
¹H NMR: environments, chemical shift and integration
Splitting patterns and the n + 1 rule

questions.q: Propan-2-ol has the molecular formula C₃H₈O. Which statement about the formula C₃H₈O is correct?
options: It is the molecular formula only, since an empirical formula is simpler.
It is a condensed structural formula, as it lists every atom present.
It identifies propan-2-ol, since no other compound has this formula.
It is both the molecular and the empirical formula of propan-2-ol.
optionWhy: A student who assumes an empirical formula must always be a reduced version of the molecular formula picks this. It is the simplest whole-number ratio, and 3:8:1 cannot be reduced, so here the two formulas are the same.
Listing every atom is not the same as showing structure. C₃H₈O gives no information about which atoms are bonded to which; a condensed structural formula for propan-2-ol is CH₃CH(OH)CH₃.
A student who treats a molecular formula as unique to one compound picks this. Propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, and methoxyethane, CH₃OCH₂CH₃, are also C₃H₈O: they are structural isomers of propan-2-ol.
The subscripts 3, 8 and 1 have no common factor, so the ratio C:H:O = 3:8:1 is already the simplest whole-number ratio. The empirical formula is therefore identical to the molecular formula.
questions.explain: The subscripts 3, 8 and 1 have no common factor, so the ratio C:H:O = 3:8:1 is already the simplest whole-number ratio. The empirical formula is therefore identical to the molecular formula.

questions.q: The skeletal formula of a compound is a zig-zag line of five straight segments joined end to end. An –OH group is drawn at the point where the first and second segments meet (the second point from the left-hand end). No other atoms are shown. What is the molecular formula of the compound?
options: C₅H₁₂O
C₆H₁₄O
C₄H₁₀O
C₆H₁₅O
optionWhy: A student who counts each line segment as a carbon atom, giving five carbons, picks this. The segments are C–C bonds; the carbon atoms are at the six points where segments end or meet.

Five segments have six points (two ends and four bends), and each point is a carbon atom, so the chain has six carbon atoms. Each carbon carries enough H atoms to make four bonds: CH₃ at each end, CH(OH) at point 2 and CH₂ at points 3, 4 and 5, giving 3 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 13 H on carbon plus 1 H on oxygen. The compound is hexan-2-ol, C₆H₁₄O.
A student who counts only the four bends as carbon atoms picks this. The two free line ends are also carbon atoms (CH₃ groups), so the chain has six carbons.

A student who gives every end carbon three H atoms and every inner carbon two, without adjusting for the carbon that carries the –OH, picks this. That carbon already has a bond to oxygen, so it has only one H atom; the total is 14 H, not 15.
questions.explain: Five segments have six points (two ends and four bends), and each point is a carbon atom, so the chain has six carbon atoms. Each carbon carries enough H atoms to make four bonds: CH₃ at each end, CH(OH) at point 2 and CH₂ at points 3, 4 and 5, giving 3 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 13 H on carbon plus 1 H on oxygen. The compound is hexan-2-ol, C₆H₁₄O.
questions.working: Carbon atoms: 5 segments give 5 + 1 = 6 points, each a carbon atom. Hydrogen atoms (4 bonds per carbon): point 1 CH₃ (3), point 2 CH bonded to OH (1), points 3–5 CH₂ (2 + 2 + 2), point 6 CH₃ (3) → 13 H on carbon; plus 1 H in –OH → 14 H. One O atom. Molecular formula C₆H₁₄O (hexan-2-ol).

questions.q: Which compound contains an ester group?
options: CH₃COOH
CH₃CH₂OCH₃
CH₃COOCH₃
CH₃COCH₂CH₃
optionWhy: A student who matches the letters COO picks this. In CH₃COOH the singly bonded oxygen carries a hydrogen atom, so this is the carboxyl group of a carboxylic acid (ethanoic acid), not an ester.
This compound has an oxygen joining two carbon atoms but no C=O. That is an alkoxy group, making it an ether (methoxyethane). An ester needs –COO–.
In CH₃COOCH₃ (methyl ethanoate) the carbonyl carbon is bonded to an oxygen atom that is bonded to a carbon atom, the –COO– ester group, R–COO–R′.
This compound has a C=O inside the chain but only one oxygen atom. It is a ketone (butanone) with a carbonyl group, not an ester, which needs –COO–.
questions.explain: In CH₃COOCH₃ (methyl ethanoate) the carbonyl carbon is bonded to an oxygen atom that is bonded to a carbon atom, the –COO– ester group, R–COO–R′.

questions.q: Which statement gives the defining feature of an unsaturated organic compound?
options: Its molecules contain at least one carbon–carbon double or triple bond.
Its molecules have fewer H atoms than the alkane with the same number of C atoms.
Some of the carbon atoms in its molecules have formed fewer than four bonds.
Its molecules contain a functional group, such as –OH or –Cl, in place of an H atom.
optionWhy: An unsaturated compound contains at least one C=C or C≡C bond. A saturated compound contains only single bonds between its carbon atoms.
A low hydrogen count is not the defining feature. Cyclohexane, C₆H₁₂, and chloroethane, C₂H₅Cl, both have fewer H atoms than the matching alkane, yet contain only C–C single bonds and are saturated.
Each carbon in a C=C bond forms four bonds: two to the other carbon and two to other atoms. 'Unsaturated' refers to the multiple bond, not to a spare, unused bond.
Having a functional group does not make a compound unsaturated. Ethanol and chloroethane have only single bonds between carbon atoms and are saturated.
questions.explain: An unsaturated compound contains at least one C=C or C≡C bond. A saturated compound contains only single bonds between its carbon atoms.

questions.q: Which pair of compounds are successive members of the same homologous series?
options: CH₃CH₂CHO and CH₃COCH₂CH₃
CH₃COOH and CH₃CH₂COOH
CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl and CH₃CHClCH₃
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃ and CH₃CH=CHCH₃
optionWhy: These differ by CH₂ (C₃H₆O and C₄H₈O), but propanal is an aldehyde and butanone is a ketone. Successive members must also share the same functional group.
Ethanoic acid and propanoic acid are both carboxylic acids (same functional group, general formula CₙH₂ₙO₂) and their formulas differ by one CH₂ unit, so they are successive members of one series.
These have the same molecular formula, C₃H₇Cl. They are structural (position) isomers, not homologues, which differ by CH₂.
Butane and but-2-ene differ by H₂ and belong to different series, the alkanes and the alkenes. A homologous series keeps the functional group and adds CH₂.
questions.explain: Ethanoic acid and propanoic acid are both carboxylic acids (same functional group, general formula CₙH₂ₙO₂) and their formulas differ by one CH₂ unit, so they are successive members of one series.

questions.q: Methanol, ethanol, propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol are successive members of the homologous series of alcohols. Which statement about these four compounds is correct?
options: They fit one general formula and have similar chemical properties.
They share a functional group, so they have the same boiling point.
They are structural isomers of each other, as each has one –OH group.
Their chemical reactions differ widely, as their chain lengths differ.
optionWhy: All four fit CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH and contain the same functional group, the hydroxyl group, so they undergo similar reactions. Their physical properties change gradually along the series.
A shared functional group gives similar chemical properties, not identical physical ones. Their boiling points rise along the series (about 65 °C, 78 °C, 97 °C and 118 °C).
Isomers need the same molecular formula. These compounds differ by CH₂ each time (CH₄O, C₂H₆O, C₃H₈O, C₄H₁₀O), so they are homologues, not isomers.
Chemical properties are set mainly by the functional group, which is the same in all four. Chain length changes physical properties such as boiling point.
questions.explain: All four fit CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH and contain the same functional group, the hydroxyl group, so they undergo similar reactions. Their physical properties change gradually along the series.

questions.q: The boiling points of four successive alcohols are: methanol 65 °C, ethanol 78 °C, propan-1-ol 97 °C and butan-1-ol 118 °C. Which statement explains this trend?
options: Longer molecules have more H atoms, so they form more hydrogen bonds.
Longer molecules contain more covalent bonds to break on boiling.
Heavier molecules need more energy to move, whatever the forces.
London forces grow with chain length; each molecule still has one –OH group.
optionWhy: Only the H bonded to O takes part in hydrogen bonding in an alcohol. Each of these molecules has one –OH group; the extra C–H hydrogen atoms do not form hydrogen bonds.
Boiling separates whole molecules; no covalent bonds inside the molecules are broken. The trend comes from stronger intermolecular forces.
Mass rises along the series, but the cause of the higher boiling point is the stronger London forces between larger molecules, which have more electrons.

Each molecule has one –OH group, so hydrogen bonding per molecule is similar across the series. Each extra CH₂ adds electrons and contact area, strengthening the London forces between molecules, so more energy is needed to separate them.
questions.explain: Each molecule has one –OH group, so hydrogen bonding per molecule is similar across the series. Each extra CH₂ adds electrons and contact area, strengthening the London forces between molecules, so more energy is needed to separate them.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CHO?
options: 3-methylbutanal
2-methylbutanol
2-methylbutanal
2-ethylpropanal
optionWhy: A student who numbers from the left-hand end as the formula is written picks this. The aldehyde carbon is always carbon 1, which puts the methyl group on carbon 2.
The suffix -ol means a hydroxyl group (alcohol). This compound has a –CHO group, an aldehyde, which takes the suffix -al.
The longest chain containing the –CHO carbon has four carbon atoms (butanal). The –CHO carbon is carbon 1, so the methyl branch is on carbon 2: 2-methylbutanal.

A student who traces the chain from the functional-group carbon into the CH₃ branch without checking the other route picks this. The longest chain containing the –CHO carbon runs through the CH₂CH₃ group and has four carbons, so the parent is butanal.
questions.explain: The longest chain containing the –CHO carbon has four carbon atoms (butanal). The –CHO carbon is carbon 1, so the methyl branch is on carbon 2: 2-methylbutanal.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂Cl?
options: 1-chloro-2-methylbutane
4-chloro-3-methylbutane
1-chloro-2-ethylpropane
2-methyl-1-chlorobutane
optionWhy: The longest chain has four carbon atoms (butane). Numbering from the CH₂Cl end gives the locant set {1, 2}, lower than {3, 4} from the other end. Prefixes are written alphabetically: 1-chloro-2-methylbutane.
A student who numbers from the left-hand end as the formula is written picks this. Numbering from the other end gives the lower locants, 1 and 2.

A student who traces the chain from the functional-group carbon into the CH₃ branch without checking the other route picks this. The longest chain runs through the CH₂CH₃ group and has four carbons; an ethyl branch on carbon 2 is a sign that a longer chain was missed.

A student who places the halogen next to the parent name, as the -ol suffix is in 2-methylbutan-1-ol, picks this. Chloro- is a prefix like methyl-, and prefixes go in alphabetical order: 1-chloro-2-methylbutane.
questions.explain: The longest chain has four carbon atoms (butane). Numbering from the CH₂Cl end gives the locant set {1, 2}, lower than {3, 4} from the other end. Prefixes are written alphabetically: 1-chloro-2-methylbutane.

questions.q: Which compound is a tertiary alcohol?
options: CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CH₃
CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂OH
HOCH₂CH(OH)CH₂OH
(CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂CH₃
optionWhy: The –OH is on carbon 3, but the class is not the locant. The carbon carrying –OH is bonded to two other carbons, so pentan-3-ol is a secondary alcohol.
This molecule has a carbon bonded to three carbons, but it is not the carbon carrying –OH. That carbon, the CH₂, is bonded to one carbon, so 2-methylpropan-1-ol is primary.
Three –OH groups do not make an alcohol tertiary. The class depends on the carbon bearing each –OH: here two are primary and one is secondary.
In 2-methylbutan-2-ol the carbon carrying –OH is bonded to three other carbon atoms (two CH₃ groups and a CH₂CH₃ group), so it is a tertiary alcohol.
questions.explain: In 2-methylbutan-2-ol the carbon carrying –OH is bonded to three other carbon atoms (two CH₃ groups and a CH₂CH₃ group), so it is a tertiary alcohol.

questions.q: Which statement about the compound (CH₃)₃CNH₂ is correct?
options: It is a tertiary amine, as the C bonded to N carries three CH₃ groups.
It is a secondary amine, as its N atom is bonded to two H atoms.
It is a primary amine, as its N atom is bonded to one C atom.
It is an amide, since an –NH₂ group is bonded to its C atom.
optionWhy: A student who uses the rule for alcohols and halogenoalkanes picks this. For amines, count the carbon atoms bonded directly to nitrogen: there is only one.
The class counts carbon atoms on the nitrogen, not hydrogen atoms. An –NH₂ group has one carbon on N and is primary.
Amines are classified by the number of carbon atoms bonded to the nitrogen atom. Here the nitrogen is bonded to one carbon (and two H atoms), so the compound is a primary amine.
An amide needs the nitrogen bonded to a carbonyl carbon (–CONH₂). The carbon bonded to N here has no C=O, so this is an amine.
questions.explain: Amines are classified by the number of carbon atoms bonded to the nitrogen atom. Here the nitrogen is bonded to one carbon (and two H atoms), so the compound is a primary amine.

questions.q: A sample of 3-methylhexane, CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃, is a racemic mixture. Which statement about the sample is correct?
options: It contains equal amounts of the cis and trans isomers of 3-methylhexane.
Its molecules are achiral, which is why the sample shows no optical activity.
It contains equal amounts of the two enantiomers of 3-methylhexane.
Fractional distillation separates it into its two enantiomers.
optionWhy: 3-Methylhexane has no C=C bond or ring, so it cannot show cis–trans isomerism. Its chiral carbon gives enantiomers, which are non-superimposable mirror images; cis and trans isomers are not mirror images of each other.
Every molecule in the sample is chiral. The sample is optically inactive because the two enantiomers rotate the plane by equal angles in opposite directions, so their effects cancel.

A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of the two enantiomers. Carbon 3 of 3-methylhexane is chiral (bonded to H, CH₃, C₂H₅ and C₃H₇), so the compound exists as a pair of enantiomers, which rotate plane-polarized light equally in opposite directions.
Enantiomers have identical boiling points, so distillation cannot separate them. They differ only in the direction in which they rotate plane-polarized light and in chiral environments.
questions.explain: A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of the two enantiomers. Carbon 3 of 3-methylhexane is chiral (bonded to H, CH₃, C₂H₅ and C₃H₇), so the compound exists as a pair of enantiomers, which rotate plane-polarized light equally in opposite directions.

questions.q: Which statement about the molecular ion peak in the mass spectrum of an organic compound is correct?
options: It is the tallest peak, as most molecules reach the detector unbroken.
It is due to an ion formed when a molecule gains an electron.
Any peak at lower m/z than it shows an impurity in the sample.
Its m/z value gives the relative molecular mass of the compound.
optionWhy: The tallest peak is the base peak, often a fragment ion. For propanone the base peak is at m/z 43 while M⁺ is at m/z 58.
The molecular ion forms when a high-energy electron knocks an electron out of the molecule, giving a positive ion, M⁺.
Peaks at lower m/z are fragment ions from the compound itself, formed when molecular ions break apart. They are evidence of its structure, not of an impurity.
The molecular ion, M⁺, is the whole molecule minus one electron. With a charge of 1+, its m/z value equals the relative molecular mass of the compound.
questions.explain: The molecular ion, M⁺, is the whole molecule minus one electron. With a charge of 1+, its m/z value equals the relative molecular mass of the compound.

questions.q: The diagram shows the mass spectrum of propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH. Which statement about the spectrum is correct?
options: The peak at m/z 31 is the molecular ion, since it is the tallest peak.
The peak at m/z 31 is formed by loss of a fragment of mass 31 from the molecular ion.
An uncharged C₂H₅ fragment gives the peak at m/z 29 as CH₂OH⁺ forms.
The base peak at m/z 31 is CH₂OH⁺, formed when the molecular ion loses C₂H₅.
optionWhy: The molecular ion is the peak at the highest m/z that corresponds to the whole molecule, m/z 60 here, and it is often small because most molecular ions fragment. The tallest peak is the most stable fragment ion.
An m/z value is the mass of the ion detected, not of the piece lost. Loss of 31 from M⁺ would give a peak at m/z 29; the peak at m/z 31 is the CH₂OH⁺ ion, left after C₂H₅ (mass 29) is lost.
Only charged particles are accelerated and detected. When CH₂OH⁺ forms, the C₂H₅ radical is uncharged and gives no peak; the peak at m/z 29 is the C₂H₅⁺ ion formed in a different fragmentation.

M_r of propan-1-ol is 60, so the molecular ion is the small peak at m/z 60. Breaking the C–C bond next to the OH-bearing carbon gives the stable ion CH₂OH⁺ (m/z 31) and an uncharged C₂H₅ fragment (60 − 31 = 29).
questions.explain: M_r of propan-1-ol is 60, so the molecular ion is the small peak at m/z 60. Breaking the C–C bond next to the OH-bearing carbon gives the stable ion CH₂OH⁺ (m/z 31) and an uncharged C₂H₅ fragment (60 − 31 = 29).
questions.working: M_r of propan-1-ol = 3 × 12 + 8 × 1 + 16 = 60, so the molecular ion is at m/z 60. CH₂OH⁺ = 12 + 2 + 16 + 1 = 31, so the base peak at m/z 31 is CH₂OH⁺; the mass lost is 60 − 31 = 29 = C₂H₅ (24 + 5).

questions.q: Carbon dioxide and water vapour are greenhouse gases, but nitrogen and oxygen are not. Which statement explains this difference?
options: CO₂ and H₂O are polar molecules, but N₂ and O₂ are non-polar molecules.
Vibrations of CO₂ and H₂O change their dipole moment, so they absorb IR.
Like the ozone layer, CO₂ and H₂O absorb the Sun's ultraviolet radiation.
CO₂ and H₂O reflect infrared radiation back to Earth, but N₂ and O₂ do not.
optionWhy: CO₂ is linear and non-polar overall, yet it is a greenhouse gas. What matters is a change in dipole moment during a vibration, not a permanent dipole.

A molecule absorbs infrared radiation when a vibration changes its dipole moment. CO₂ (asymmetric stretch and bending) and H₂O have such vibrations and absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface. N₂ and O₂ have none.
The greenhouse effect involves infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface. Absorption of ultraviolet radiation by ozone is a separate process.
Greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation, which makes their bonds vibrate, and then re-emit it in all directions. They do not act as a mirror.
questions.explain: A molecule absorbs infrared radiation when a vibration changes its dipole moment. CO₂ (asymmetric stretch and bending) and H₂O have such vibrations and absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface. N₂ and O₂ have none.

questions.q: Which describes the ¹H NMR spectrum of 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH?
options: one signal, as only H atoms on carbon give signals
two signals, with areas in the ratio 1:1
two signals, whose areas are in the ratio 9:1
ten signals, one for each H atom in the molecule
optionWhy: The hydrogen of the –OH group also gives a signal, so there are two signals, not one.
The number of signals is right, but the area under each signal is proportional to the number of H atoms in that environment: 9 for the CH₃ groups and 1 for OH, not 1:1.
The nine hydrogen atoms of the three equivalent CH₃ groups form one environment, and the O–H hydrogen forms a second. Two signals, with areas in the ratio 9:1.
Each chemical environment gives one signal, not each hydrogen atom. The nine CH₃ hydrogen atoms are equivalent and give a single signal.
questions.explain: The nine hydrogen atoms of the three equivalent CH₃ groups form one environment, and the O–H hydrogen forms a second. Two signals, with areas in the ratio 9:1.

questions.q: The diagram shows the low-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum of propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, with the relative area of each signal. Typical chemical shifts: R–O–CH₂–, 3.3–3.7 ppm; R–OH, 1.0–6.0 ppm; R–CH₃, 0.9–1.0 ppm. Which statement is correct?
options: The signal at δ 3.6, of area 2, is the CH₂ group bonded to the oxygen atom.
The signal at δ 2.3, of area 1, cannot be the O–H hydrogen, since O–H hydrogens give no signal.
The four signals should have equal areas, since each stands for one chemical environment.
The signal at δ 3.6 is the CH₃ group, since the group with most H atoms has the largest shift.
optionWhy: Hydrogen atoms in R–O–CH₂– appear at 3.3–3.7 ppm, and the –CH₂OH group has two hydrogen atoms, matching the 2H signal at δ 3.6.
Every hydrogen atom gives a signal, including the one bonded to oxygen. The single O–H hydrogen gives the 1H signal at δ 2.3, within the R–OH range.
The area under a signal is proportional to the number of hydrogen atoms in that environment: 3 (CH₃), 2 (CH₂), 2 (CH₂O) and 1 (OH), which is what the spectrum shows.
Chemical shift depends on the environment, not on the number of hydrogen atoms. The signal at δ 3.6 has area 2, and the 3H signal is at δ 0.9, in the R–CH₃ range.
questions.explain: Hydrogen atoms in R–O–CH₂– appear at 3.3–3.7 ppm, and the –CH₂OH group has two hydrogen atoms, matching the 2H signal at δ 3.6.
questions.working: Relative areas 3 : 2 : 2 : 1 match CH₃ (3H), CH₂ (2H), CH₂O (2H) and OH (1H). The signal at δ 3.6 lies in the 3.3–3.7 ppm range for R–O–CH₂– and has area 2, so it is the –CH₂OH group.

questions.q: In the ¹H NMR spectrum of butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃, which splitting pattern does the signal from the CH₃ group bonded to the carbonyl carbon show?
options: a quartet, as the CH₃ group itself contains three H atoms
a singlet, as the adjacent carbon has no H atoms
a doublet, as its carbon is bonded to one other carbon atom
a triplet, as it is split by the two H atoms of the CH₂ group
optionWhy: In the n + 1 rule, n counts H atoms on the neighbouring carbon atoms, not in the group itself. Here the neighbouring carbon has none.
The only carbon adjacent to this CH₃ group is the carbonyl carbon, which has no hydrogen atoms. With n = 0 neighbouring H atoms, the signal is a singlet (n + 1 = 1).
n counts hydrogen atoms on neighbouring carbons, not the number of neighbouring carbon atoms. The carbonyl carbon has no H atoms, so there is no splitting.
The CH₂ group is on the other side of the carbonyl carbon, not on an adjacent carbon. Only H atoms on adjacent carbons cause splitting; the CH₂ splits the other CH₃ signal into a triplet.
questions.explain: The only carbon adjacent to this CH₃ group is the carbonyl carbon, which has no hydrogen atoms. With n = 0 neighbouring H atoms, the signal is a singlet (n + 1 = 1).

questions.q: In a high-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum, one signal is split into a quartet. What does this show about the structure?
options: The carbon atom(s) adjacent to the group carry three hydrogen atoms in total.
The group giving the signal is a CH₃ group, since its three H atoms give 3 + 1 = 4 peaks.
The carbon atom giving the signal is bonded to three other carbon atoms in the chain.
The environment giving the signal contains four equivalent hydrogen atoms.
optionWhy: By the n + 1 rule, four peaks means n = 3 hydrogen atoms on the adjacent carbon atom(s), for example a CH₂ group next to a CH₃ group. The number of hydrogen atoms in the group itself is shown by the area, not the splitting.
n in the n + 1 rule counts hydrogen atoms on the neighbouring carbon atoms, not in the group itself. A CH₃ group next to a carbon with no hydrogen atoms gives a singlet.
Splitting is caused by hydrogen atoms on adjacent carbon atoms, not by the number of atoms bonded to the carbon of the group. n counts neighbouring H atoms.
The number of hydrogen atoms in an environment is given by the area under the signal. Four peaks means three hydrogen atoms on the adjacent carbon atom(s), whatever the size of the group itself.
questions.explain: By the n + 1 rule, four peaks means n = 3 hydrogen atoms on the adjacent carbon atom(s), for example a CH₂ group next to a CH₃ group. The number of hydrogen atoms in the group itself is shown by the area, not the splitting.

questions.q: Compound X, C₄H₈O₂ (M_r = 88), gives these data. IR: sharp absorptions at 2850–3000 cm⁻¹, a strong absorption at 1740 cm⁻¹ and no broad absorption (ranges: C–H 2850–3090 cm⁻¹; C=O 1700–1750 cm⁻¹; O–H in carboxylic acids 2500–3000 cm⁻¹, very broad). MS: M⁺ at m/z 88 and a peak at m/z 29 (CHO⁺ or C₂H₅⁺). ¹H NMR: δ 1.3 (triplet, 3H), δ 2.0 (singlet, 3H), δ 4.1 (quartet, 2H); H on a carbon bonded to the singly bonded O of an ester, –C(=O)–O–CH₂–, appears at 3.7–4.8 ppm. Which identification is consistent with all the data?
options: Ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃: the δ 4.1 quartet is a CH₂ bonded to the ester O and to a CH₃.
Methyl propanoate, CH₃CH₂COOCH₃: its CH₃, CH₂ and OCH₃ give a triplet, quartet and singlet.
Butanoic acid, CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH: the bands at 2850–3000 and 1740 cm⁻¹ are its O–H and C=O.
Propyl methanoate, HCOOCH₂CH₂CH₃: the peak at m/z 29 identifies its HCO group.
optionWhy: IR shows C=O (1740 cm⁻¹) and no O–H. In CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ the O–CH₂ group appears at δ 4.1 (3.7–4.8 ppm) as a quartet (3 H on the adjacent CH₃), the CH₃ of the ethyl group is a triplet, and the CH₃CO group is a singlet; its ethyl group gives C₂H₅⁺ at m/z 29.

The splitting and areas match, but the shifts do not. In CH₃CH₂COOCH₃ the OCH₃ singlet would appear near δ 3.7 and the quartet (CH₂ next to C=O) near δ 2.3; the spectrum has the singlet at δ 2.0 and the quartet at δ 4.1.
Sharp bands at 2850–3000 cm⁻¹ are C–H absorptions. A carboxylic acid would give a very broad O–H band across 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ and a ¹H NMR signal at 9.0–13.0 ppm; neither is present.
m/z 29 could be CHO⁺ or C₂H₅⁺, so it does not decide. HCOOCH₂CH₂CH₃ would give four ¹H NMR signals, not three, and no 3H singlet.
questions.explain: IR shows C=O (1740 cm⁻¹) and no O–H. In CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ the O–CH₂ group appears at δ 4.1 (3.7–4.8 ppm) as a quartet (3 H on the adjacent CH₃), the CH₃ of the ethyl group is a triplet, and the CH₃CO group is a singlet; its ethyl group gives C₂H₅⁺ at m/z 29.
